newsitem.title: UK: Dlr firm in Europe awaiting US data, focus on stg.
newsitem.headline: Dlr firm in Europe awaiting US data, focus on stg.

text.p: The dollar was firm against the mark and yen in Europe's morning trade, though moves were small as the market awaited U.S. payrolls data due this afternoon and turned its attention to sterling following the British election.

Britain's Labour party won power for the first time in 18 years in an overwhelming victory in Thursday's polls. A Labour win had been fully expected, but the scale of its majority over the Conservatives took many by surprise.
In the 659-seat UK parliament, Labour had won a majority of almost 180 with all but 31 seats counted.
Sterling firmed against the dollar and mark overnight as the Labour party swept to power, but had come under pressure by early European trade.
Dealers cited a column in the Times newspaper on Friday which said Britain's new government "must create conditions for an immediate fall in the pound" to avoid economic damage.

The pound was at $1.6027/37 and 2.7590/00 marks at 0740 GMT, off peaks of $1.6280 and 2.8035 reached overnight and down from $1.6236/42 and 2.7935/45 in late European trade on Thursday before the poll results.
The dollar, meanwhile, was little affected by the British election, moving in ranges of about half a pfennig and half a yen during the overnight session.
It was at 1.7228/33 marks and 126.57/67 yen against 1.7198/03 and 126.60/65 in late Europe on Thursday.

Analysts said the currency market's focus would remain on sterling's moves until the U.S. payrolls data at 1230 GMT today, with the dollar expected to drift until then. The sheer size of Labour's majority would make international investors nervous about sterling because of perceptions the ruling party might have a freer hand in carrying out radical policies, they said.

"The sheer size of the victory has taken some of the shine off the pound already and that could continue...but although it's coming off a bit, it's still going to remain pretty firm in the near term," said Gerard Lyons, chief economist at DKB International here.
"Once the new Chancellor (finance minister) convinces the markets that his policies are not going to be radical, sterling should pick up a bit," Lyons said.
Regarding the dollar, analysts said a strong payrolls number was unlikely to give the currency much of a boost, adding that a softer number was likely to have more of an impact.
Key U.S. economic data so far this week have made the market waver concerning expectations of an imminent interest rate hike.

The April NAPM report yesterday showed a drop in indices on business activity and prices, while first-quarter GDP growth on Wednesday far outstripped forecasts. Employment costs dropped according to data released on Tuesday.

"We're in a situation in which interest rate expectations and bond yields have begun to move against the dollar. The dollar has been supported so far by inflows into the bond and equity markets, but the pattern tends to be of short-term predominance," said Chris Turner, currency strategist at BZW.
"Eventually the dollar will come down in line with interest rate expectations. Another weak number today in the non-farm payrolls could see the dollar move down," Turner said.
The April headline payrolls figure is forecast to rise by 211,000 after an increase of 175,000 in March, while the unemployment rate is expected to be unchanged at 5.2 percent.
